`parse(input, options)` reads a query string, with or without a leading `?` or `#`, into an object. Pairs are separated by `&`, empty pairs are skipped, and each pair splits at its first unencoded `=`, with a missing `=` meaning an empty value. Keys and values are decoded separately: `+` stands for a space unless `options.plusAsSpace` is false, percent escapes are decoded, and text that cannot be decoded is kept as it is. A key is split into a path on its unencoded brackets before any decoding, so `a[b][c]` nests but an encoded bracket stays part of a name; `options.depth` (5 by default) limits how many bracket groups are structural, and whatever is left of the key becomes one final literal segment. Empty brackets append to the container, a repeated plain key collects its values into an array in order, and a container whose keys are all non-negative integers written without leading zeros becomes an array, ordered by index with missing indices dropped, as long as the largest index is below `options.arrayLimit` (20 by default). Every key is stored as an own property, so `__proto__` never reaches a prototype, and each call returns a result no earlier call can observe or influence.

`stringify(input, options)` writes an object back. Members are written in insertion order, or ordered by their whole written key when `options.sort` is true, comparing by code unit. Strings, numbers and booleans become their text, `undefined` members are skipped, and a `null` member writes its key with no `=` at all unless `options.skipNull` is set, which drops it. Keys and values are percent-encoded, including `!'()*`, with structural brackets left literal and spaces written as `%20` or, under `space: 'plus'`, as `+`. `extract(url)` returns the text after the first `?` that comes before any `#`, or the empty string. You implement one program task in the workspace you are given, against its own test suite, and you stop when the tests pass.

The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.

Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

All 14 tests in `test/query-string.test.js` now pass, and `node_modules` was not created. Here's a summary of the faults I found and fixed in `src/query-string.js`:

1. **Keys were decoded before splitting on brackets** — `keyPath` called `decodeComponent` on the whole raw key up front, so an encoded bracket (`%5B`/`%5D`) turned into a literal `[`/`]` and got treated as structural nesting instead of staying part of a literal name (e.g. `a%5Bb%5D=c` wrongly became `{a:{b:'c'}}` instead of `{'a[b]':'c'}`). This also meant `+` in a bracket segment was decoded even when it shouldn't be tied to that path's semantics correctly. Fixed by splitting the raw (still-encoded) key on unencoded `[`/`]` first, and decoding each resulting segment individually afterward.

2. **`plusAsSpace` was applied inconsistently to keys** — the call site passed `options.plusAsSpace === true` (default `false`) into `keyPath` instead of the already-computed `plusAsSpace` value (default `true`), inverting the default behavior for keys (e.g. `a+b=c+d` failed to turn `+` into a space in the key). Fixed by passing the correctly computed `plusAsSpace` through.

3. **Off-by-one in the array-limit check** — `compact` used `Math.max(...indices) > arrayLimit` instead of `>= arrayLimit`, so an index equal to the limit (e.g. index `20` with default limit `20`) was incorrectly still converted to an array rather than staying an object. Fixed the comparison to `>=`.

4. **`null` values in `stringify` were written as `key=` instead of bare `key`** — `collect` pushed `value: ''` for `null` members, and the final join always wrote `=value`. Fixed by pushing `value: null` as the marker, which the existing join logic (`pair.value === null ? pair.path : ...`) already correctly renders as the bare key.

5. **Unwanted cross-call memoization in `parse`** — a module-level `parsed` Map cached results by input string and returned the *same* object/array references on repeated calls, which violated "each call returns a result no earlier call can observe or influence" (mutating one parse result corrupted subsequent calls with the same input). Removed the memoization entirely so every call builds a fresh tree.

All fixes were confined to `src/query-string.js`; no test files, `package.json`, or dependencies were touched, and no special-casing of specific test inputs was introduced — each fix addresses a general logic error per the spec.

`src/query-string.js` is a finished reader and writer for URL query strings, and its test suite is failing. Find and fix the faults in the module. Keep every behaviour the passing tests already pin down, keep the exported names `parse`, `stringify` and `extract`, and do not weaken the module by special-casing the inputs the tests happen to use.

`parse(input, options)` reads a query string, with or without a leading `?` or `#`, into an object. Pairs are separated by `&`, empty pairs are skipped, and each pair splits at its first unencoded `=`, with a missing `=` meaning an empty value. Keys and values are decoded separately: `+` stands for a space unless `options.plusAsSpace` is false, percent escapes are decoded, and text that cannot be decoded is kept as it is. A key is split into a path on its unencoded brackets before any decoding, so `a[b][c]` nests but an encoded bracket stays part of a name; `options.depth` (5 by default) limits how many bracket groups are structural, and whatever is left of the key becomes one final literal segment. Empty brackets append to the container, a repeated plain key collects its values into an array in order, and a container whose keys are all non-negative integers written without leading zeros becomes an array, ordered by index with missing indices dropped, as long as the largest index is below `options.arrayLimit` (20 by default). Every key is stored as an own property, so `__proto__` never reaches a prototype, and each call returns a result no earlier call can observe or influence.

`stringify(input, options)` writes an object back. Members are written in insertion order, or ordered by their whole written key when `options.sort` is true, comparing by code unit. A nested object writes `a[b]=x`; an array writes `a[0]=x` by default, `a[]=x` under `arrayFormat: 'brackets'` and `a=x` under `arrayFormat: 'repeat'`; an empty array or object writes nothing. Strings, numbers and booleans become their text, `undefined` members are skipped, and a `null` member writes its key with no `=` at all unless `options.skipNull` is set, which drops it. Keys and values are percent-encoded, including `!'()*`, with structural brackets left literal and spaces written as `%20` or, under `space: 'plus'`, as `+`. `extract(url)` returns the text after the first `?` that comes before any `#`, or the empty string. Bad arguments throw `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.
